Guernsey Container Port Operations Disrupted by Major Cyber Attack

Guernsey’s economic activity has been severely disrupted by a sophisticated cyber attack targeting the island’s main container port at St. Sampson, with port operations at a standstill for the second consecutive day. The attack, first detected early Tuesday morning, has rendered critical port management systems inoperable, halting the unloading and dispatch of goods and causing widespread knock-on effects across Guernsey.

According to the Guernsey Maritime Authority, the attack disabled scheduling, customs and inventory databases, leaving dozens of cargo vessels unable to offload shipments. “We are working with our cybersecurity response partners and the States of Guernsey to restore access, but at this point, all container handling remains suspended,” said Andrew Le Page, the Authority’s chief executive. “Our priority is to resume operations safely and securely, but we cannot yet provide a timeline.”

The port is a crucial gateway for the island’s supply chain, handling roughly 90 percent of Guernsey’s imported goods. As a result, supermarkets have reported gaps in shelves and rationing of certain household staples, while construction sites have warned of imminent shortages in building materials. “We’re already seeing delays to projects and increased costs because scheduled deliveries can’t be processed,” said Julie Renouf, spokesperson for the Guernsey Construction Federation. “If disruption continues, we could see work grinding to a halt by the end of the week.”

Financial services firms, which employ a significant portion of Guernsey’s workforce, have also been affected. “Key documentation and equipment for client onboarding are stuck at the port,” said a director at Sarnian Trust Services, a local trust administration provider. “We’re working around the clock to mitigate delays, but the impact is significant.”

The Guernsey Chamber of Commerce has called for emergency measures, including prioritised ferry shipments and alternative routing for critical supplies. The States of Guernsey confirmed it is coordinating with UK authorities and cybersecurity experts from the National Cyber Emergency Response Centre.

The full scale and origin of the attack remain unclear, with authorities declining to comment on attribution while investigations are ongoing. Local unions have called for urgent support for workers facing lost hours and uncertainty.

“We are treating this as a national emergency,” said Home Affairs Minister Sophie Bourgaize. “Our immediate focus is maintaining essential services and supporting businesses and residents throughout the disruption.”
